skip_reason: Inbound escalation/service-recovery call from an existing repeat customer, not a sales or quoting call. Susan Rubio called to report that she had cancelled a job already in progress that morning in San Antonio after a crew member was rough with her belongings, chipped a nightstand, and walked off swearing. The entire call is complaint intake, apology, crew accountability, and a promise to have the San Antonio manager call back. No quote form recap, no pricing, no clock explanation, no estimate, no Save Your Ass prep speech, and no booking — Alexander explicitly deferred the rebooking ('let me go ahead and just make sure that I reach out to the manager that star in San antonio') and told her 'I'm quite sure we wouldn't charge you for, for, for probably any labor at all.' Existing-customer logistics with zero quoting, so the 85-point sales scorecard does not apply.
top_strength: For a call that is not gradeable on the sales rubric, Alexander handled the escalation about as well as the transcript allows. He let a very upset repeat customer talk for several uninterrupted minutes without cutting in, then named the standard clearly rather than making excuses: 'Yeah, this is definitely not how we do things. And I'm very sorry about this experience that you guys had.' He was transparent about his own position instead of pretending to be local — 'I'm answering the call right now remotely from Houston. I do, work pretty often with, with the San antonio branch' — which set honest expectations for what he could resolve himself. He proactively took the billing question off the table before she had to fight for it ('I'm quite sure we wouldn't charge you for, for, for probably any labor at all'), offered the claim twice even after she waved it off ('are you sure you don't want to do the claim?'), and validated the part that actually mattered to her — the sentimental loss, not the dollar value: 'they damaged, you know, an item with sentimental value. All of, all of the items should have been handled with care. You know, considering the context and they knew better once you communicated that.' He also correctly separated the one good crew member from the three bad ones ('it seems like Tyler was the only one that was treating you with the DC that you deserve'), which tells her the feedback is being heard specifically, not generically. He closed by confirming the callback number, setting urgency ('I want to reach out to him immediately right now'), and holding a tomorrow slot as a safety net even after she said she might find another mover — 'I just wanna make sure that we have that available in case you need us.' She ended the call warmer than she started it: 'Yeah, thank you so much. I appreciate it.'
coaching_note: Not scored — this is escalation handling, not a sales call, and it should be routed to claims/ops review rather than counted in the sales grading average. Two coaching points for the escalation path itself. First, the highest-leverage miss: Alexander accepted 'It's, I don't need to file a clump a, a claim or anything like that' at face value and let the damaged nightstand die on the call. On a sentimental-value damage from a repeat customer, the right move is to file it anyway and tell her so: 'Susan, I'm going to log this under our No Worries Damage Coverage on my end regardless — you don't have to do anything, and if you decide later you want the nightstand repaired, it'll already be documented. I'd rather have it on file than not.' A verbal waiver on an emotional call is not a durable record, and if she changes her mind next week there is nothing to point to. Second, he never took an explicit note-back or committed to a written follow-up. He promised three separate things verbally — no labor charge, a manager callback, and a held crew for tomorrow — and none of them are confirmed in writing to the customer. The line to add before hanging up: 'I'm sending you a quick email right now with what I've committed to — no charge for today, [manager name] calling you back this afternoon, and a crew held for tomorrow — so you have it in writing and can reply if I've got anything wrong.' Third, smaller: he got crew names secondhand and guessed at two of them ('Yeah, it should be Ashton', 'that must been Tyler'). On a formal complaint, confirm the actual crew roster from the job record before echoing names back, so the write-up names the right people. Business risk to close today: Susan said 'I know they got on the phone with him' about the San Antonio manager — meaning the crew's version of this morning may already be the only version on file. Amanda should make sure the customer's account reaches that manager independently and that the no-charge commitment is actually entered before the job bills.
phone_presence_notes: Consistently warm and de-escalating under a genuinely hot complaint — real empathy markers ('Oh, my god', 'Wow. Okay', 'I completely understand and I'm very sorry about that ma'am'), no defensiveness, and the customer's tone softened to 'thank you so much, I appreciate it' by the close; held back from a 5 only by heavy verbal stumbling and repeated filler that made several commitments hard to follow.
audio_review_reason: Emotionally charged escalation with a Bluetooth connection the customer warned was failing ('my Bluetooth is getting ready to go'), plus noticeably disfluent rep speech on the key commitment sentences ('we wouldn't charge you for, for, for probably any labor at all'). Worth an audio listen both to verify the de-escalation actually landed in tone and because this call is a candidate for crew-conduct review, where the customer's exact account matters.
